=== SLIDE 1
Deload to Reload


…and other stuff
 === SLIDE 2
The human body

  The human body is nothing more than an
  interdependent matrix system that
  communicates with and amongst itself all
  day long through electronically charged
  molecules-you are an ever evolving and
  fluctuating organism that is self-regulating
  and supercompensating-you are nothing
  more than a bio-electrical field that is hell
  bent on one function---SURVIVAL!
 === SLIDE 3
Horse/Carrot Theory

  ALL programs work-they only work for
   so long-NOTHING works forever!
  To adapt is not to adapt (Louie
   Simmons)
  Definition of adaptation
 === SLIDE 4
Adaptation
  Hans Selye-GAS (Stress of Life)
  3 stages (Alarm-Resistance-Exhaustion)
  Body does NOT differentiate stressors-all stress is stress and is
   accumulative over time
  Only differentiates between Local and General
  Stress response of the body is greater for training than it is for a broken
   bone (general vs. local)
  Training affects 7 different biological systems (omegawave)
      Cardiac
      Cardiopulmonary
      Hormonal
      Detoxification
      Metabolic
      CNS
      neuromuscular
  All these systems DO NOT adapt at the same time
  Adaptation is also NOT an equilibrium process (Verkoshansky)
 === SLIDE 5
Adaptation (con’t)

  Is a phenomenon of accommodation
     characterizes the organism’s entire reaction

     reflects the specific features of the external
      influences
  It is the active maintenance of a definite level
   of disequilibrium between the organism and
   the environment
     The fundamental reason for the origin and
      development of accommodative reconstruction
      within the organism (Verkoshansky).
 === SLIDE 6
NOBODY has it figured out
  ALL programs are flawed
    training is by nature incomplete

  No perfect training variable
  No two people respond the same to the same
   stimulus
  No one best exercise for anything - they are
   all stimulus’ to be used
  There are those who the only difference
   between them and GOD is God knows he is
   not them
 === SLIDE 7
Recovery
  REST at some point in time becomes an
   actual training methodic
  Recovery/ restoration begins with a well
   conceived program that allows for
   recovery
    It is the first means of recovery!!!

  The optimal load applied during a period of
   supercompensation (deload week) creates
   a summation/ additive affect that aids in
   stabilizing the increase in performance
 === SLIDE 8
Other stuff I believe
   There is the opinion of the expert, the opinion of the
    coach, the opinion of the athlete and finally the opinion of
    the athlete’s body
   The athlete’s body is ALWAYS right-their bodies talk to
    you during every workout –are YOU listening???
   As a coach you should be dynamic and above all flexible
   Everything I know I have learned and I change my mind
    on certain things on a daily bases (stole from Mike Boyle)
   Increase in volume or intensity must increase amount of
    recovery
   Introducing a new exercise also is a means to increase
    intensity
 === SLIDE 9
Reasons for deloading
  Stolen from Jim Wendler’s article on Elitefts
  Give the body a rest (replenish CAR)
       take advantage of supercompensation
  Give the mind a rest
  Prevent overtraining-yes Joe Weider & the barbarian
   brothers there is such a thing
  Strength training athletes are prone to overtraining
   from too much volume (addisonic-sympathetic
   inhibition)-which usually occurs in endurance athletes
   and from too much intensity (basedowic-sympathetic
   over activity)
  Christian Thibaudeau articles on T-nation detail this
   more and is a great source of info
 === SLIDE 10
Reasons for deloading
  Prevent injury (McGill applied load –tissue tolerance-
   safety zone)
  Increase chance of progress
     STABILIZE new level of performance if you set a PR in
      training
     shut it down and do not train at that new PR immediately
     allow for the body to accept that new level of increase

  Speed and strength levels fluctuation on a daily basis
     max effort is what you have for that day
     you will not break PR’s every time you perform the same
      max effort exercise
 === SLIDE 11
Examples of deloads
    Deload every 4 weeks-either the 4th week or the 3rd week
    Performance block (USA weightlifting) wk 1-70/6x4 wk2 -77/4x4 wk3-65/7x3
     wk4-85/2x5
    Base-load-load-deload wk1-75/5x4 wk2-77/4x4 wk3-80/3x5 wk4-70/4x4
    Performance base wk1-72/3x6 wk2-80/2x8 wk3 67/3x6 multiple rep max
     based on a training intensity from a previous 1rep max
    Zatsiorsky performs 60% of their highest volume for the training cycle on the
     unload week as a rule of thumb-switches lifting to Tues/Thurs and MB
     circuits/tempo work on Mon-Wed-Fri. Decreases the volume of work to the CNS
     and unloads the joints. His belief that the extra tempo flushes the system and
     aids in restoration process
    Wk 1-70/4-6x3 wk2-80/3-6x4 wk3-75/3-6 wk4-85/2-4x5
    Wk1-70/4-6x3 wk2-75/4-6x4 wk3-80/3-6x5 wk4-70/4x3
    Unload from max effort 4 weeks followed by 2weeks of high rep db work 2x20
     with 5min rest intervals
    Max effort work is based on 1rep max of exercise/classical example-floor press
     is 92% of 1rep bench max for an athlete
    Max effort exercises follow partial/ full movement scheme ex. Floor press-
     incline press-3 board- close grip bench- 2 board- weight releasers (80/60-6x1
     5min.rest intervals
 === SLIDE 12
Weekly template
    Train Offensive / Defensive Line like throwers
    Train Skill / Linebackers / Tight Ends like sprinters
    Monday
       active/ dynamic warm-up
       Speed mechanics/drills (as part of a/d warm-up)
       Wall acceleration position
       Speed training (Charlie Francis short to long program)
       Example:
       1st 3 weeks hills for acceleration 10/10 10sec rest-2mins- 10/20 20sec rest-
         2mins-2/30 30sec rest (skill only)
       Total volume of speed training is between 300-500 yards
       Strength training, pre/rehab, squat, posterior chain work (2 exercises),
         jumps before or after (primer or pap)
       Post mobility work/stretch static
       Core stabilization exercises/ timed method
       Strength training guidelines with exception of rehab/ prehab work, NO
         MORE than 3-5 exercises
 === SLIDE 13
Weekly template
  Tuesday
    Prehab/ rehab work/cuff-neck-traps
    MB or iso holds
    Upper body training
    Max effort exercise
    Assistance exercise for chest (pap)
    Rowing/ back exercise
    Upper back
    (option) light triceps work low intensity-higher volume/reps, 2-3sets
     10-15reps
    Abs/ repetition method
    Active/ dynamic warm-up followed by conditioning, example
     2min/3min, yardage based on position
    Mobility exercises/ work, static stretch
 === SLIDE 14
Weekly template
  Thursday
    Active/dynamic warm-up

    Speed mechanics/drills

    Wall acceleration position

    Speed training-same volume of work as Monday (as
     they adapt to workout will change sets and reps )
    Strength training, dynamic effort method (OL / DL, LB /
     TE)
    Skill  uni-lateral movements (start with BB lunge)

    Post mobility work/stretch static

    Core stabilization/timed method
 === SLIDE 15
Weekly template
  Friday
    Pre/rehab work/cuff-neck-traps
    Upper body plyometrics (MB’s, altitude drops, isoballistics, depth
     drop push-ups)
    Dynamic bench press (start with isomiometrics-then progress to
     reactive/speed method-3week waves straight weight, chains and
     bands)
    Tricep emphasis 1- 2exercises (close grip board presses-db tricep
     extensions)
    Back exercise / vertical pull
    Shoulders/variations of posterior delt raises-lateral raises
    Abs/repetition method
    Active/dynamic warm-up followed by conditioning (progresses from
     timed work/rest intervals to Fartleks to tempo work)
    Mobility exercises/static stretch
 === SLIDE 16
Conclusion
  Once the body stops learning the body stops growing
  How you perform or present an exercise to the body
   is oft times more important than the actual exercise
  Bruce Lee- Having no way as way and no limit as
   limit (disregard what is useless and retain what is
   useful)
  Always search for the Holy Grail and realize there is
   no magic formula or magical programs
     there are many means and methods. Use them all!
     there are always ways to improve your training program (if
      and only if you are willing to be open-minded)
  Train optimally not maximally
 === SLIDE 17
Sanity

  The following people are held responsible for
   maintaining my sanity:
    Louie Simmons and all of the Westside athletes
     (which includes Dave Tate and Jim Wendler)
    Tom Myslinski, Allan deGennaro, Paul Childress,
     Charlie Francis, My Sportster and Harley
     Davidson, most of all Mike Hope who without I
     would have begun a heroin addiction years ago!
 === SLIDE 18
Websites

  Elite fitness system (elitefts.com)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).

Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.

Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

Tags added 2026-09-28 from the method interview:

- **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric stated or claimed the position in the interview. His words are quoted as "Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Qn):". ## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- General rule for any test or technology, stated as a standing rule rather than a fresh call each time. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)**
- The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)**
- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
- Attribution in practice: outside frameworks are absorbed into the team's own way of working rather than credited to one person. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q27): "We fold it into the mantra of 'this is how we do our business.'" **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q27)** Inference: this is how Eric applies the "we/our" bullet above, so that bullet reads as practice, though the transcript line itself is still unclaimed.
- The "five expectations" culture rules (Golden Rule, Be Disciplined, Be Relentless, Communicate, No Excuses) were presented in the course as absolute [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.1-2]. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q26): "These are more a relic of another coaching era that has held over. I would say none [no deliberate exception], but they are rarely mentioned around here any more." **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q26)**
- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]

## Department model and roles

- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
- Asked whether Applied Performance is a peer discipline that enables Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine and Nutrition, or in-house programming support for Athletic Performance, Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q5): "Both." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q5)** Resolves Tension 2.
- Coach-facing reports are built by whoever supports the team, which for most teams is strength staff. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams. When applicable, sport science staff would provide it." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q28)**
- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]

## Testing and assessment

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7] (See the cadence bullet below: there is no department-wide cadence.)

- Change of direction is not tested in most sports. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q13): "If the data is captured, it's on an individual sport basis and that information lives with that coach." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q13)** The RTP templates still gate on COD and FMS, run by Athletic Medicine or the sport coach (Tension 18, resolved 2026-10-02).
- The Assessment Manual V12 is not current. A new, more robust manual is in development and will incorporate the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)** Every bullet below sourced to `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md` is therefore Legacy.
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status: "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q10)**: no sport tests true 1RM now; was Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]

## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds, not a single cut-off or position-group thresholds. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2): "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized." Individualized against: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)** Inference: "should be" may describe the intended rule rather than a fully running one; no numeric threshold was given. See Tension 12 (daily testing versus a Wednesday read), resolved 2026-10-02: daily jumps build the baseline and SWC, Wednesday is the decision read.
- The dynamic strength index (DSI: CMJ against isometric mid-thigh pull peak force) chooses between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q21): "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** This is not the SJ-CMJ gap the question asked about. Evidence check done 2026-09-29 (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`): cite it as Eric's practice, tagged [contested; the ratio tracks IMTP strength; one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data]. See Tension 17.
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Load monitoring and GPS

- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary; it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2] The formal gap is confirmed. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q7)** The question also asked about informal thresholds; that half was not answered.
- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. ## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

## Strength and power

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + shared course material) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky), matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + slides) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. - Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15] Inference: with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes. Kept on that explicit basis (Tension 16, resolved 2026-10-02).
- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days; a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25] Inference: consistent with Eric siding with Issurin (Q16), whose strength residual is 30 ± 5 days, though Q16 was about speed and he did not claim this bullet.
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]; claimed again in the interview, **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**
- Glycolytic conditioning is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q19): "It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm

# The Rule of Sixty Percent: A Light Day or Week Carries About 60% of a Heavy One's Volume

**What it is** — "The *gradual overload principle*, with periodic underloading days or microcycles, is constantly adhered to through all training cycles to ensure that an adequate, but not excessive, training stimulus is imposed on the body. A preliminary recommendation is that individual workouts should generally be alternated in terms of light, medium and heavy loading to guard against overtraining and to ensure optimal training and competitive efficiency. This variation in training load on a daily, microcyclic and mesocyclic basis is essential for avoiding stagnation. In this respect, it is

**Why it works** — The authors call it "empirical" and give no mechanism or source. The surrounding rationale is guarding against overtraining and stagnation.

**When to apply** — When writing a light day or deload week and needing a default size for it relative to the heavy unit. Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the rule gives one number for the "low" week in that wave.

**When NOT to apply** — It specifies volume only; the page says nothing about whether intensity also drops on the light stage. The rule is not tested on this page and no population is named. The authors give no figure for a "medium" stage. Inference: in Vorobyev's printed weekly distributions on PDF p. 333 the lightest week is well under 60% of the heaviest (for example 15% versus 37% of a month's load in Fig 6.3A, about 41%), so the book's own examples do not all follow the rule.

**Example** — Inference: if a heavy microcycle totals 20,000 kg of squat and pull volume, the rule puts the following light microcycle at about 12,000 kg.

**Related** — [[claim--heavy-medium-light-alternation-beats-monotonic-increasing-loading]], [[case-study--vorobyev-ermakov-weightlifting-load-distributions]], [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]]

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete

**Why it works** — The authors call it "empirical" and give no mechanism or source. The surrounding rationale is guarding against overtraining and stagnation.
